title: A Talk at a Science Museum
description: Four recordings from a day at a science museum: a welcome announcement, a dinosaur tour, a chat between students and a talk about bees.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Welcome to the museum
parts.intro: You will hear a member of staff welcoming visitors to a science museum.

script.speaker: Ms Green
script.text: Welcome to the Discovery Science Museum. I'm Ms Green, and I'll tell you what's happening today.

script.speaker: Ms Green
script.text: The museum has three floors. The dinosaur hall is on the ground floor, the space gallery is on the first floor, and the Invention Lab is at the top. The lift is out of order today, so please use the stairs or the ramp near the café.

script.speaker: Ms Green
script.text: At eleven o'clock, there's a free show called Lightning in the Lab. It was supposed to be in room four, but it's been moved to the main theatre because so many people have booked.

script.speaker: Ms Green
script.text: The planetarium costs an extra three pounds and shows a film about the planets every hour on the hour. The last show today is at four o'clock.

script.speaker: Ms Green
script.text: Lunch is available in the café, but you're welcome to eat your own sandwiches in the garden. Please don't eat in the galleries, because food can damage the exhibits.

script.speaker: Ms Green
script.text: Finally, if you get lost, ask any member of staff in a yellow shirt. Have a wonderful day.

parts.title: Part 2 · The dinosaur hall
parts.intro: You will hear a guide, Dan, talking to a teacher, Mrs Lee, in front of a dinosaur skeleton.

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: This is our most famous exhibit, the skeleton of a long-necked dinosaur. It's twenty-two metres long.

script.speaker: Mrs Lee
script.text: It's enormous, Dan. How do scientists know how old it is?

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: Good question. They study the rock around the bones. This one was found in a desert, and it's about a hundred and fifty million years old.

script.speaker: Mrs Lee
script.text: And is it complete?

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: Not quite. About sixty per cent of the bones are real. The rest, including the skull, were made from plastic, because the original skull was never found.

script.speaker: Mrs Lee
script.text: That's surprising. My students will be disappointed.

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: I wouldn't worry. Most children are more excited when they learn how scientists work it out. Actually, in the corner you'll find a table where you can touch real fossils.

script.speaker: Mrs Lee
script.text: That sounds ideal. Can the children take photos?

script.speaker: Dan
script.text: Yes, but without flash, please. It can harm some of the older displays. And if they'd like to draw the dinosaur, we have free pencils and paper at the desk.

script.speaker: Mrs Lee
script.text: Wonderful. Thank you so much.

parts.title: Part 3 · Students and the worksheet
parts.intro: You will hear two students, Peter and Linh, talking about their museum worksheet.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Linh, have you finished the worksheet? I'm stuck on question six.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Which one's that? The one about the mirror room?

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Yes. It asks why the room looks bigger than it is.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Because mirrors on every wall reflect the light again and again, so it looks like the room goes on forever. I wrote that down, and then I took a photo of it.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Ah, of course. I thought it was because of the lights on the ceiling.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: That's what I assumed at first, too, but the guide corrected me.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Fine. By the way, did you try the robot arm?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: I did. It was harder than it looks. I tried to pick up a cup, and I knocked it over three times.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: I managed it on my second try. I think I'm a natural.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Don't get too proud. You dropped your sandwich in the café, remember? Anyway, shall we do the quiz in the gift shop? There's a free pencil if you finish.

script.speaker: Peter
script.text: Sure. Let's go.

parts.title: Part 4 · A talk about bees
parts.intro: You will hear a scientist, Dr Patel, giving a talk in the museum.

script.speaker: Dr Patel
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Dr Patel, and I study bees. Today I'd like to show you something that surprised scientists for many years.

script.speaker: Dr Patel
script.text: Bees can't speak, but they communicate with a special movement called the waggle dance. When a bee finds a good source of flowers, it returns to the hive and dances in a figure of eight.

script.speaker: Dr Patel
script.text: The angle of the dance tells the other bees which direction to fly, using the sun as a guide. The longer the dance lasts, the further away the flowers are.

script.speaker: Dr Patel
script.text: For a long time, people thought this was just a nice story. It was only in the nineteen sixties that a scientist proved it by following the bees with tiny marks of paint.

script.speaker: Dr Patel
script.text: Sadly, bee numbers are falling in many countries, mainly because of the loss of wild flowers and the use of strong chemicals on farms. Without bees, a third of our food would disappear.

script.speaker: Dr Patel
script.text: So what can you do? Plant flowers on your balcony or in your garden, and avoid using chemicals. Even small actions can help. Now, who has a question?
